synopsis: The manufacturer is developing automatic braking when an operator fails to react to a proximity warning; the principal documented fatal accident pattern is a large machine moving forward over an unseen person or light vehicle [f1, f2977]. Powered haulage accounted for 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%) and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal mining injuries (9%) in calendar 2025 [f2979, f2980]. Validation must span different machine sizes and sensor positions, potentially 100 or more sites and applications, while stopping depends heavily on terrain; machine types, brake systems and other essential manufacturer inputs remain unknown [f8256, f11376, f11374, f5863, f8]. The research found neither a complete numeric off-road automatic-braking type-approval test nor a standard accepting simulation instead of physical testing, although ISO 21815-1:2022 covers relevant machinery classes, ISO 3450:2011 specifies earth-moving brake performance tests, and South Africa’s Regulation 8.10 was the strongest explicit off-road automatic-braking mandate found [f2147, f7539, f2149, f10651, f2277]. Major evidence gaps include simulated stopping-distance validation on difficult terrain and public demonstrations combining heavy machines, varied geometries, more than 100 site types, severe weather, soiling and closed-loop braking; highway-to-quarry transfer remains uncertain, and road-vehicle mileage requirements do not transfer numerically [f3743, f4409, f45, f6664]. The roadmap faces a hard deadline and a first-time capability build: past physical testing and tuning took three to four years per model, no quantified off-road reduction in physical testing was found, and expert advice calls for representative sensors and machines before the final validation window [f9400, f9401, f7507, f7563, f4460].
